A storm wrecks your ship. You must decide what to save.

For three days your vessel had held her course without incident; then, towards evening, the wind began to rise. By midnight the little ship was labouring among enormous seas, climbing each black ridge only to plunge into the gulf beyond.

Without warning, a violent shock ran from stem to stern. The hull had struck a submerged rock. You heard timber give way below, and presently the unmistakable rush of water entering the hold. Already the deck was settling beneath your feet.

There was no time to save the ship. One object, perhaps, might be carried through the surf. Which would you choose?
wash ashore
You reach the shore with the knife still in hand.

You leap with the knife firmly grasped in your hand. The icy water drives the breath from your lungs; a breaker overwhelms you, and a second follows before you can recover. Yet each time you regain the surface, the blade remains in your possession.

How long this struggle lasts you cannot determine. At length your knees strike sand. You crawl beyond the reach of the waves and remain motionless, still clutching the one useful instrument rescued from the wreck.
wash ashore
You reach the shore with your matches.

You secure the little tin of matches beneath your shirt and abandon the sinking vessel. The sea receives you with a cold that seems to stop the heart. Wave after wave turns you helplessly, until even the direction of the surface becomes uncertain.

A final swell bears you forward and casts you upon the sand. With considerable effort you drag yourself above the tide. Your first thought is for the tin: it is still closed, and there may yet be fire within your reach.
wash ashore
You reach the shore with your rescued provisions.

You take up the bag of provisions and leap from the deck. The cold water closes over you. A wave nearly wrests the bag away, but you wind its strap about your wrist and struggle towards the dark outline of the shore.

The breakers fling you upon the sand. There you lie for some moments, scarcely conscious, the sodden provisions still attached to your arm. Carefully husbanded, they may suffice for three days.
wash ashore
You struggle ashore carrying the water can.

You seize the full water can and spring into the sea. Its weight hinders every movement, though its slight buoyancy affords a precarious support. Clinging to it, you endure the waves as they break above your head.

At last the ground rises beneath your feet. You stagger out of the surf, the can held close, and fall upon the beach. The vessel is lost; this small provision, at least, has survived.
